content: The 2022 revised Korean guidelines for postpolypectomy colonoscopic surveillance provide detailed recommendations for managing patients who have undergone polypectomy, with a focus on reducing the risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) and advanced neoplasia. 1. Purpose of the Guidelines: These guidelines aim to optimize postpolypectomy surveillance by identifying high-risk factors for metachronous CRC and advanced neoplasia. They are based on a comprehensive review of evidence and are tailored to the Korean healthcare environment. The recommendations are designed to balance the benefits of surveillance with the risks of complications and resource limitations. 2. High-Risk Findings for Metachronous CRC: The following are considered high-risk findings that warrant closer surveillance: Adenomas ≥ 10 mm in size. Presence of 3–5 or more adenomas. Tubulovillous or villous adenomas. Adenomas with high-grade dysplasia. Traditional serrated adenomas (TSAs). Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) with any grade of dysplasia. Serrated polyps ≥ 10 mm in size. Presence of 3–5 or more SSLs. 3. Significance of Colonoscopy in CRC Prevention: Colonoscopy is a critical tool for CRC screening and prevention. Polypectomy during colonoscopy significantly reduces CRC incidence and mortality. However, patients with a history of polyps remain at increased risk for future polyps and CRC, necessitating appropriate surveillance. 4. Surveillance Intervals: Surveillance intervals are determined based on the size, number, and histological features of the polyps removed during the index colonoscopy. For example: Patients with high-risk adenomas (e.g., adenomas ≥ 10 mm or with high-grade dysplasia) should undergo surveillance colonoscopy within 3 years. Patients with low-risk findings may have longer intervals between surveillance colonoscopies. 5. Histological Risk Factors: Tubulovillous and Villous Adenomas: These adenomas are associated with a higher risk of advanced neoplasia and CRC compared to tubular adenomas. Villous histology, in particular, is a significant risk factor. Serrated Polyps: Serrated polyps, especially SSLs ≥ 10 mm or with dysplasia, are high-risk lesions. TSAs are also considered high-risk due to their potential for malignant transformation. SSLs with Dysplasia: These lesions have a higher risk of progression to CRC and warrant closer surveillance. 6. Size and Number of Polyps: Larger polyps (≥ 10 mm) and a greater number of polyps (≥ 3) are associated with an increased risk of advanced neoplasia. Patients with > 10 adenomas may have a genetic predisposition (e.g., familial adenomatous polyposis) and should be evaluated for hereditary syndromes. 7. Piecemeal Resection: Piecemeal resection of large polyps (≥ 20 mm) is associated with a higher risk of incomplete resection and local recurrence compared to en bloc resection. Early follow-up colonoscopy is recommended in these cases to ensure complete removal and monitor for recurrence. 8. Limitations of the Guidelines: Most evidence is derived from studies conducted in Western populations, with limited data specific to the Korean population. Observational studies, rather than randomized controlled trials, form the basis of much of the evidence, which may limit the strength of the recommendations. 9. Development Process: The guidelines were developed through a systematic review of international guidelines and evidence, followed by consensus discussions among experts. The recommendations were adapted to the Korean clinical context and will be revised as new evidence emerges. 10. Implementation and Monitoring: The guidelines will be disseminated through professional societies and journals. Efforts will be made to monitor changes in clinical practice and treatment patterns following their implementation. 11. Conflicts of Interest and Funding: The development of the guidelines was supported by the Korean Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, with no undue influence on the content. All authors disclosed potential conflicts of interest, and none were involved in the peer review process for this article. 12. Key Recommendations: Surveillance intervals should be tailored to individual risk factors, including polyp size, number, and histology. High-quality colonoscopy with adequate bowel preparation is essential for accurate risk assessment and effective surveillance. Genetic testing should be considered for patients with multiple adenomas or a family history of CRC. These guidelines provide a comprehensive framework for postpolypectomy surveillance, emphasizing evidence-based practices to reduce CRC risk while considering the unique characteristics of the Korean healthcare system.
